clue.text: Crayons may have been put in this place, since moving

definitions.text: Crayons may have been put in this

indicators.note: things that are moving are being shifted about, so the letters before it change places

parts.note: the two words taken letter for letter, ignoring the comma

explanation.surface: Someone explains why the crayons were packed away: the family is moving house.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma splits 'place' from 'since' in the surface, but the two words are read together as one set of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A pencil case is the small zipped container a schoolchild keeps pens, pencils and crayons in.

clue.text: See 19
Snatch forty winks in break, after saying goodbye to son

indicators.note: bidding farewell to something means it leaves, so the letter for son departs from the word

parts.note: to snap is to break suddenly
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A worker grabs a quick doze during a tea break.
explanation.walkthrough: SNAP loses its S to leave NAP.
explanation.definitionFit: To nap is to have a short sleep, which is what snatching forty winks idiomatically means.

clue.text: Eventually qualified for a marathon?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: over a lengthy period, ultimately
second meaning, read literally: entered in a race of great distance

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful literal reading: a runner who has qualified for a marathon is taking part in a lengthy race.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means ultimately or over time, while the literal words describe competing in a race of great distance.

clue.text: Tribe's leader one English newspaper featured in series

indicators.note: something featured in a work appears inside it, so the short pieces sit within the word for series

parts.note: a chain of events is a series
the Roman numeral for one
E is the usual abbreviation for English
the Financial Times, a British daily paper

explanation.surface: A tribal head gets written up in a run of articles in an English paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Featured in series' reads as a newspaper feature, but it tells you to put pieces inside another word; the FT is the Financial Times.
explanation.definitionFit: A chieftain is the head of a clan or tribe, so the word names its leader.

clue.text: Argument from group against

parts.note: a set is a group of things or people
as in a ladder put to the wall, set against it

explanation.surface: A dispute arises from a faction that is opposed to something.
explanation.definitionFit: A set-to is an informal word for a quarrel or brief fight, so it is a kind of argument.

clue.text: Fish from shop, a haddock

indicators.note: the answer is taken out of the run of letters that follows, spanning the word boundaries

parts.note: the letters run across shop and a and haddock

explanation.surface: Buying a haddock at the fishmonger's.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers haddock as the fish, but the actual answer is a much rarer one tucked inside the words.
explanation.definitionFit: The opah, or moonfish, is a large brightly coloured ocean fish.

clue.text: Actor's role, one I strongly criticise in court

parts.note: an actor's role is his or her part
the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: pieces placed in something sit inside it, so the earlier pieces go within the abbreviation for court

parts.note: CT is the abbreviation for court
taken as written
critics pan a show they dislike

explanation.surface: An actor admits panning a performance while in court.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is split off the definition: 'Actor' alone is defined, and the possessive belongs to the wordplay word that follows it. Note there are two I's, one from 'one' and one from 'I'.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor is someone who takes part in something, and a participant is likewise one who participates or acts in it.

clue.text: Males relaxing inside now in a Surrey town

indicators.note: the rearranged letters are placed within the word that follows

parts.note: as in 'the moment is here', meaning at the present time

indicators.note: relaxing loosens things up, so the letters of the word before it come out of their order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Men unwinding in a commuter town south-west of London.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is a county just south-west of London; Haslemere is a market town at its southern edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Haslemere is a town in the county of Surrey, so the definition names its location and kind.

clue.text: Write in detail about king in exile

indicators.note: one word placed about another surrounds it, wrapping round the letter for king

parts.note: to expatiate is to speak or write at length
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A writer produces a detailed account of a banished monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: An expatriate lives outside their native country, which is the situation of anyone living in exile.

clue.text: Sensitive over a London landmark

indicators.note: in a down-style flip, turning something over reads it from its far end, so the word for sensitive runs backwards

parts.note: a sore spot is a sensitive one

explanation.surface: A touchy visitor fussing over a famous London sight.
explanation.walkthrough: The statue in Piccadilly Circus is popularly called Eros.
explanation.definitionFit: The winged statue atop the Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain in Piccadilly Circus is a famous London sight known by this name.

clue.text: Morsel, pretty poor for a seabird

indicators.note: something poor is in bad shape, so the letters before it are knocked out of order

parts.note: both words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A small, rather miserable scrap of food thrown to a gull.
explanation.definitionFit: The storm petrel, or stormy petrel, is a small dark seabird of the open ocean.

clue.text: Bird dog heading off

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter, and off says that letter is removed

parts.note: a beagle is a breed of hunting dog

explanation.surface: A bird dog setting off to hunt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird dog' reads as a gun dog, but Bird is the definition and dog the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The eagle is a large bird of prey, so it is a straightforward example of a bird.

clue.text: Clotho given spread — a horror story

indicators.note: spread out means scattered, so the letters are dispersed into a fresh order

parts.note: both words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Clotho, the Fate who spins the thread of life, is given a spread of something scary.
explanation.walkthrough: Clotho is one of the three Fates of Greek myth; her name is only here for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gothic novel, such as Frankenstein or Dracula, is the classic genre of horror fiction.

clue.text: Outcome of bitter suffering around pole?

definitions.text: Outcome of bitter suffering around pole?

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go around the letter for a pole, enclosing it
something suffering is in a bad way, so the letters before it are thrown into disorder

parts.note: the two words taken letter for letter
S for south, one of the poles of a compass

explanation.surface: Wondering what comes of enduring bitter cold near the North Pole.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: bitter cold endured near a pole results in frostbite. 'Outcome' looks like the definition alone, but the wordplay starts at 'of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Frostbite is tissue damage caused by extreme cold, the typical injury of explorers enduring polar conditions.

clue.text: What conscripts had to do, subject to check

parts.note: a subject of a country is one of its nationals
a car's service is a routine check
joins the two pieces

explanation.surface: Conscripts had to submit to inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: National service was compulsory military service in Britain until 1960.
explanation.definitionFit: Conscripts were required to perform a period of compulsory military duty, which Britain called national service.

clue.text: Airborne, flying around noon — it requires little thought

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go around the letter for midday, holding it inside
things flying about are in disorder, so the letters of the word before it are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
N is short for noon

explanation.surface: Taking a midday flight is an easy decision.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-brainer is an informal term for a decision so obvious that it needs no real thought.

clue.text: Bottom pinched by admirer, Observer employee?

indicators.note: something pinched by another is gripped inside it, so the word for bottom is held within the word for admirer

parts.note: a suitor is a would-be lover or admirer
the bottom of a river or sea is its bed

explanation.surface: A cheeky admirer pinches a bottom, while someone looks on.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer is a British Sunday newspaper, so an employee there might be a subeditor; the question mark marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A subeditor checks and corrects copy at a newspaper such as the Observer, so is one example of its staff.

clue.text: Unspecified number in bundle — bargains, possibly, from a charity event

indicators.note: the variable is placed within the next word, inside its letters
possibly signals that the letters before it are one possible arrangement of something else

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
in algebra, x, y and n stand for unknown quantities

explanation.surface: A bundle of bargains, of no stated size, picked up at a fundraiser.
explanation.walkthrough: A bring-and-buy sale is a British charity sale where people donate goods and buy others' donations.
explanation.definitionFit: A bring-and-buy sale is a fundraising event, often for a church or charity, where donated items are sold.

clue.text: There's little weight on girl, daughter declared

indicators.note: in an across answer, one piece written on another comes after it

parts.note: a girl's name
an ounce is a small unit of weight
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A girl's daughter says she is slim.
explanation.definitionFit: To announce something is to state or declare it publicly.

clue.text: Conservative speeches I prepared for bishop, say

indicators.note: prepared speeches are worked up, so the letters are reworked into something new

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Tory politician writes speeches for a churchman.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the bishop a cleric, but the 'say' marks it as an example of a game piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The bishop is one of the pieces in chess, so it is an example of a chess piece.

clue.text: Come into section of garden terrace

indicators.note: a section is one part of the whole, so the answer is a stretch of the letters that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of garden and the start of terrace

explanation.surface: Stepping on to part of a terrace in the garden.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter a place is to come into it, a plain synonym.

clue.text: One may be saddled with a supplementary clause

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a horse's ... sits in a saddle
second meaning: an addition attached to a bill or contract

explanation.walkthrough: 'Saddled with' reads as being burdened, but saddled stands alone: a horseman sits in the saddle.
explanation.definitionFit: One who rides a horse sits in the saddle, and the same word names an extra clause attached to a document.

clue.text: Wheel hub and what sounds like jack

indicators.note: the answer is pronounced the same as the word that follows, though spelt differently

parts.note: the jack in a pack of cards is also called the knave

explanation.surface: A wheel's hub paired with a jack, as if listing parts from a car toolkit.
explanation.walkthrough: The jack in playing cards is also called the knave, and the K is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: The nave of a wheel is its central hub, an old technical word for the part the spokes radiate from.

clue.text: Unwisely retreated, I said again

indicators.note: doing something unwisely means doing it badly, so the letters come out in a muddled order

parts.note: the word and the pronoun taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone repeats a confession that they foolishly withdrew.
explanation.definitionFit: To reiterate is to repeat, so reiterated means said once more.

clue.text: Some bust a gut to get a ticket

indicators.note: some means only a portion of what follows, so the answer is a run of letters within it

parts.note: the letters run across the end of bust, a and the start of gut

explanation.surface: Some people strain themselves to obtain a ticket.
explanation.definitionFit: A tag is a label attached to something, much as a ticket on goods shows its price.

clue.text: First to recommend Cambridgeshire city bank

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of recommend
Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, in eastern England

explanation.surface: Advice to recommend a bank in a Cambridgeshire city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' is a verb here: to bank on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To bank on someone is to depend on them, so bank, as a verb, is a synonym of rely.

clue.text: One ought to know a lot about houses

definitions.text: One ought to know a lot about houses

parts.words: One ought to know a lot about houses
parts.note: surface reading: an estate agent or surveyor with property expertise
setter's reading: the twelve houses of the zodiac chart, read by a stargazing fortune-teller

explanation.walkthrough: Houses suggests property, but in horoscopes the sky is divided into twelve houses.
explanation.definitionFit: A horoscope caster divides the heavens into twelve houses, each governing an area of life, so must know them well.
